reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / orbital disease literature
clinicalPearls: A benign non-infective, non-neoplastic inflammatory process of the orbit that is a diagnosis of exclusion
Typically presents with acute painful proptosis, periorbital swelling, redness and restricted eye movements
Any orbital structure may be involved, giving subtypes such as myositis, dacryoadenitis, anterior, diffuse and apical disease
A rapid and often dramatic response to corticosteroids is characteristic and supports the diagnosis
It must be distinguished from thyroid eye disease, orbital cellulitis, IgG4-related disease and neoplasia including lymphoma
Imaging shows inflammatory infiltration, and biopsy is indicated for atypical, recurrent or steroid-resistant cases
reference.pathophysiology: Idiopathic orbital inflammation is a polymorphous inflammatory infiltration of orbital tissues without an identifiable local or systemic cause. It is considered immune-mediated, with a mixed inflammatory infiltrate and variable fibrosis affecting the extraocular muscles, lacrimal gland, orbital fat or apex. The inflammation and mass effect produce pain, proptosis and restricted motility, and some cases overlap with, or are later reclassified as, IgG4-related disease or a defined systemic inflammatory disorder.
additionalInvestigations: CT or MRI of the orbits to define the pattern of inflammation
Thyroid function and thyroid antibodies to exclude thyroid eye disease
Orbital biopsy for atypical, recurrent or treatment-resistant disease
redFlags: Poor or absent response to corticosteroids suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Progressive visual loss from apical or optic nerve involvement
Features suggesting lymphoma or systemic vasculitis
Bilateral disease raising suspicion of a systemic cause
reference.prognosis: Many cases respond rapidly to corticosteroids, but relapse is common and some require steroid-sparing immunosuppression or radiotherapy; sclerosing variants can cause lasting fibrosis and dysfunction.
pitfalls: Accepting the diagnosis without excluding infection, thyroid eye disease and neoplasia
Attributing a steroid-responsive orbit to pseudotumour when it is lymphoma
Overlooking IgG4-related disease as an underlying cause
Failing to biopsy atypical or recurrent disease
